intro: To apply a heading style in Word on Mac, select the text, then on the Home tab choose Heading 1, Heading 2 or Heading 3 in the Styles group. The fastest route is the keyboard: select the line and press ⌘⌥1, ⌘⌥2 or ⌘⌥3 for Heading 1 to 3.
tldr: Select the heading text, then click Heading 1, Heading 2 or Heading 3 on the Home tab in the Styles group.
On Mac, the heading shortcuts are ⌘⌥1, ⌘⌥2 and ⌘⌥3. Press ⌘⇧N to return a line to Normal.
If the style you need is hidden, click the down arrow next to the Styles gallery to expand it.
Check your heading levels in Outline view with ⌃⇧ and a level number.
Microsoft labels its steps for updating a heading look as Windows steps, so confirm that option on your Mac.

blocks.text: Apply a heading style from the Styles gallery

Start on the Home tab. The Styles group shows a row of named styles, including Normal for body text and Heading 1, Heading 2 and Heading 3 for headings. The row is a gallery, so it may show only part of the list. If the style you want is not visible, click the down arrow next to the Styles gallery to expand it. Then click the style name. Word applies it to the text you selected. Microsoft's heading steps for Word for Microsoft 365 for Mac and Word 2024 for Mac follow this same path.

Select first, then choose the style. Microsoft's instructions use that order, and it keeps you from guessing which line the style touched. Triple-click a line to select the whole paragraph, or drag across the words. Then open the Home tab. A heading style applies to the whole paragraph, so make sure your selection covers the full line you want styled.
Use the keyboard shortcuts for Heading 1, 2 and 3

Microsoft's keyboard shortcut table lists three heading shortcuts for Word on Mac. Command+Option+1 applies Heading 1. Command+Option+2 applies Heading 2. Command+Option+3 applies Heading 3. In symbols, that is ⌘⌥1, ⌘⌥2 and ⌘⌥3. Press the keys together with the text selected. On Windows, the same styles use Ctrl+Alt+1, Ctrl+Alt+2 and Ctrl+Alt+3. The shortcut is quicker than the gallery when you move through a long file, because your hands stay on the keyboard.

blocks.caption: Heading and Normal shortcuts from Microsoft's Word keyboard shortcut table

blocks.text: Normal has its own shortcut, Command+Shift+N, written ⌘⇧N. Use it to turn a heading back into body text. Select the line and press the keys. The line returns to Normal, and you can apply the right heading level from there. This beats hunting through the gallery when you fix a whole document.
Pick the right heading level for each part

Heading 1 marks the biggest parts of a document. Heading 2 sits under Heading 1, and Heading 3 sits under Heading 2. Think of the levels as steps deeper into an outline. Heading size is a separate question. Word may show Heading 1 larger than Heading 2 by default, but the level tells Word and readers where a section belongs. You can change the font size later without changing the level.
Worked example: a short project report

Say you write a project report in Word for Mac. Type the title first. Then type the main section names, such as Overview, Timeline, Risks and Next steps. Select Overview and press ⌘⌥1. Do the same for Timeline, Risks and Next steps. Under Timeline, add subheadings such as Schedule and Owners. Select each one and press ⌘⌥2. If a detail under Schedule needs its own label, use ⌘⌥3. Then check the outline before you send the file.

The result reads like an outline. Each main section is a Heading 1, and each detail sits under the section it belongs to. Readers can scan the names and find the part they need. Headings also make it easier to revise a file later, because you can see where each section starts and stops.
Why skipped heading levels cause problems

Skipping a level means a Heading 1 is followed straight by a Heading 3. In a short memo, the gap is easy to miss. In a long file, it breaks the structure that headings are meant to show. WebAIM's 2026 analysis of the top 1,000,000 home pages found skipped heading levels on 41.8% of pages, up from 39% in 2025. That study covers web pages, not Word files. The lesson still applies. Keep levels in order, so screen reader users and skimming readers can follow the outline.
Check your heading structure in Outline view

Outline view shows the document as a list of headings. Microsoft's shortcut table lists the pattern as Control+Shift+ followed by a heading level number. Press ⌃⇧1 to show Heading 1 items only, and ⌃⇧2 to show headings at level 2. Use this to spot a Heading 2 that sits under the wrong Heading 1, or a section that skips a level. Scrolling through the whole file hides those problems.
Change the look of a heading without breaking the style

Changing a heading's font or color is not the same as changing its style. If you format one heading by hand, only that heading changes. A change to the style updates every paragraph that uses it. Microsoft's article says to customize a heading, then right-click its style in the Styles group and choose Update Heading to Match Selection. That article labels those steps as Windows steps. Check whether your Mac shows the option before you rely on it.

A Microsoft Q&A thread, answered by MVPs, says Word for Mac has no Manage Styles dialog and lacks some style tools that Word for Windows has. Those answers point to templates for lasting changes. Styles saved in a .dotx or .dotm template apply to every document based on that template. For the template steps, see [How to create a template in Word on Mac](/how-to/create-a-template-in-word). Editing template XML is an advanced route, so most people should skip it.
Common mistakes with heading styles

The most common mistake is faking a heading. You make a line bold and larger, but leave the style as Normal. It looks like a heading. Word does not treat it as one, so it does not appear in Outline view or in a table of contents. Apply the real heading style first, then adjust the look if you need to.

The second mistake is choosing a level by font size. Heading 1 is a structure level, not the biggest text on the page. Body text should stay Normal, even when it looks important. The third mistake is skipping levels to get a smaller look. Fix the look with the style settings instead, and keep the levels in order.

A fourth mistake is putting full sentences into a heading. A heading names a section. If the line reads like a sentence you would write in a paragraph, keep it Normal and move the main point into the text below it.

items: Did you select the full heading line before you chose the style?
Is the line bold or large by hand, with the style still set to Normal?
Did you pick the level that fits the part, not the size you want?
Is the file open in Word for Mac, not a copy in another app?
Does Outline view show the heading at the level you expect?

blocks.text: Check your Word version and recent changes

Microsoft's release notes list 16.114.3 as the latest Office for Mac build. That entry, dated October 27, 2026, lists quality and performance improvements only. The three most recent entries, from October 22 to October 27, 2026, list no changes to styles, the ribbon or the Styles pane. If your steps stop matching this page, a recent update is an unlikely cause. Check your build against the release notes, then compare your Home tab with the steps above.
Word for the web and older versions

Microsoft's heading article lists Word for Microsoft 365 for Mac, Word 2024 for Mac and the Word web app under Applies To. A second Microsoft article lists Word 2021 and Word 2024 for Mac. The Home tab steps match across the Mac versions, as far as those pages say. Microsoft's pages give no web-specific steps, so treat the Word web app as unverified here. Older versions may lay out the ribbon differently, so check your own Home tab before you assume a step is wrong.
What to do after you apply heading styles

Headings do more than look neat. They give the document a map. Word can build a table of contents from them, and the steps are in [How to insert a table of contents in Word on Mac](/how-to/insert-a-table-of-contents-in-word). If the file goes to other people, consistent headings help reviewers find a section fast. Keep the same level rules across every file in a project, so readers learn the pattern.

Before you send a file, open Outline view and read the heading names in order. If the names form a clear outline, the structure is working. If a name only makes sense inside its section, rename it so it stands alone.

faq.question: Where are heading styles in Word on Mac?
faq.answer: They sit on the Home tab, in the Styles group. Select your text, then click Heading 1, Heading 2 or Heading 3. If the style is hidden, click the down arrow next to the Styles gallery to expand it.

faq.question: What is the Mac shortcut for Heading 1?
faq.answer: Command+Option+1, written ⌘⌥1. Heading 2 is ⌘⌥2 and Heading 3 is ⌘⌥3. Microsoft's keyboard shortcut table lists these for Word on Mac.

faq.question: How do I turn a heading back into normal text?
faq.answer: Select the text and press ⌘⇧N to apply the Normal style. Microsoft lists that shortcut for Normal in its Word keyboard shortcut table for Mac.

faq.question: Can I see all my headings at once?
faq.answer: Yes, use Outline view. Press Control+Shift+ and a heading level number, such as ⌃⇧1, to show headings at that level. Microsoft lists this pattern for Word on Mac.

faq.question: Do these steps work in Word 2024 for Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft lists Word 2024 for Mac in the Applies To section of its heading article, and the Home tab steps are the same. Older versions may differ, so check the version you run.

faq.question: Why is my heading missing from the table of contents?
faq.answer: A table of contents uses heading styles. If the text is only bold or larger, Word does not see it as a heading. Apply Heading 1, 2 or 3 to the line, then update the table of contents.

faq.question: Can I change how a heading style looks on Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft describes an option called Update Heading to Match Selection, but its steps are labeled as Windows steps. Confirm that the option appears on your Mac. For lasting changes across documents, edit a template.

task: Apply heading styles in Word on Mac
appliesTo: Word for Microsoft 365 for Mac and Word 2024 for Mac
requirements: Word for Microsoft 365 for Mac or Word 2024 for Mac
A document with the text you want to format as headings
The ribbon showing the Home tab

steps.name: Open the document
steps.text: Open the Word document in Word for Microsoft 365 for Mac or Word 2024 for Mac. Find the line you want as a heading, or type a new line where you need one. Keep the cursor on that line.

steps.name: Select the whole heading line
steps.text: Triple-click the line to select the whole paragraph, or click at the start and drag to the end. Check that the highlight covers every word in the heading.
steps.tip: Partial selections are easy to miss in long text. Zoom in if the line is small on screen.

steps.name: Open the Home tab
steps.text: Click the Home tab in the ribbon. The Styles group holds the heading styles you need. You do not need any other tab for this task.

steps.name: Expand the Styles gallery if needed
steps.text: Look for Heading 1, Heading 2 and Heading 3 in the Styles group. If the style you want is not visible, click the down arrow next to the Styles gallery to expand it.
steps.tip: Microsoft's steps also mention left, right and down arrows for moving through more styles.

steps.name: Click the heading level
steps.text: Click Heading 1 for a main section, Heading 2 for a subsection under it, or Heading 3 for a smaller part. The selected text changes to that style.

steps.name: Use the shortcut instead
steps.text: With the text still selected, press ⌘⌥1 for Heading 1, ⌘⌥2 for Heading 2 or ⌘⌥3 for Heading 3. Your hands stay on the keyboard, and you skip the gallery.

steps.name: Check the outline
steps.text: Use Outline view to see your headings together. Press ⌃⇧1 to show Heading 1 items only, or ⌃⇧2 to show headings at level 2.
steps.tip: Outline view helps you find a Heading 2 that sits under the wrong Heading 1.

steps.name: Return text to Normal
steps.text: If a line has the wrong style, select it and press ⌘⇧N. The line returns to the Normal style. Then apply the heading level you meant.

steps.name: Match a heading look to its style
steps.text: Format the heading the way you want it. Right-click its style in the Styles group and choose Update Heading to Match Selection, if your Mac shows that option.
steps.tip: Microsoft labels these steps as Windows steps, so check the option on your Mac before you rely on it.

shortcuts.action: Show Heading 1 items in Outline view
Show headings at level 2 in Outline view

troubleshooting.problem: The heading style does not appear in the gallery.
troubleshooting.fix: Click the down arrow next to the Styles gallery to expand it, then look again. You can also select the text and press ⌘⌥1 to ⌘⌥3.
Select the heading text first, and confirm Word for Mac is the active app. Press the keys together again. If it still fails, apply the style from the Styles group instead.

troubleshooting.problem: My heading still looks like body text.
troubleshooting.fix: The style may be applied, but the font or color was set by hand on top of it. Select the heading and apply the style again. If the look is still wrong, remove the manual formatting from that line.

troubleshooting.problem: Update Heading to Match Selection is missing on my Mac.
troubleshooting.fix: Microsoft labels those steps as Windows steps, so Mac support for that option is not confirmed. Change the look in a template instead, or check Microsoft's current Mac help.

troubleshooting.problem: A heading level does not show in Outline view.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm the paragraph has a heading style and not just bold text. Then press Control+Shift and the matching level number again.

troubleshooting.problem: Word for the web looks different from these steps.
troubleshooting.fix: Microsoft lists the web app under Applies To, but its web-specific steps were not verified here. Start with the Home tab, and check Microsoft's Word for the web help if the steps do not match.
